$comment: Test fixture: eight resources between them exercising every recipe role against testdata/shapes/widgets.json. `widget` is the full lifecycle (create, two reads, a mutation, map-shaped tags, an authored operation, list, delete); `cog` is setup-only and its create cannot be bound, so `spare`, which requires it, has its whole group refused with setup-refused; `gauge` is pre-existing and shows that such a resource carries more than its read, and its tags carry KMS's {TagKey, TagValue} spelling; `sprocket` requires `gauge`, verifies its create with an authored assertion rather than a derived read-back, carries {Key, Value}-shaped tags, and is declared async so every clause that calls the service again — authored ones included — is wrapped in `eventually`; `valve` is pre-existing like `gauge`, and its tags pair ordinary {Key, Value} tags with an ELB-style untag list of key-only structures instead of bare strings; `hub` is pre-existing too, and its tag operations take the resource identifier as a list (HubNames) bound from the resource's own scalar export through a wrapped `binds` entry.

neverProbe.GetWidgetSecret: Rotates the secret it returns, so the read verb in its name is a lie; every later reader of the old secret is broken by the call.
neverProbe.PurgeWidgets: Purges every widget in the account and cannot be undone. It takes no identifier, so no curated literal could make the call miss; the only safe probe is none.

allowProbe.PingWidgets: A liveness check: it takes no input, changes nothing, and returns the service's own status.
allowProbe.ScanWidgets: A read AWS happens to spell with a different verb, as DynamoDB does with Scan; it lists widgets and changes nothing.

operations.$comment: PolishWidget returns nothing, so its own response says nothing about whether it worked; the read-back is the whole assertion. The resource is not async, so the clause is emitted as written.

resources.$comment: Setup-only, and deliberately unbindable: CreateCog.Name is a patterned string with no bind, no matching export and no curated literal, so instantiating this resource is refused and every group that requires it is refused with it.

A second widget, complete in itself, whose only problem is that it requires `cog`. Its group is refused as setup-refused:cog before a single test is emitted — the refusal names the resource that could not be set up, and the operation it names is the create that would otherwise have been fine.

Pre-existing: no create, no delete, and its exports come from its read. Its group is not that read alone — an authored operation binding one of those exports gets a test of its own. Its tags are the {TagKey, TagValue} spelling KMS uses (Tag/ListResourceTags/UntagResource), paired with an ordinary string-list untag — the same untag shape `widget` and `sprocket` use, so this resource isolates the tag-structure axis of detectTagShape from the untag-list axis `valve` isolates below.

Pre-existing, like `gauge`, and exists only to carry a tags block: ordinary {Key, Value} tags (the same structure `sprocket` uses) paired with an untag member that takes a list of key-only structures instead of bare strings — the shape ELB Classic's RemoveTags uses. This isolates the untag-list axis of detectTagShape from the tag-structure axis `gauge` isolates above.

Pre-existing, like `gauge` and `valve`, and the resource that carries a list-shaped identifier: TagHub, DescribeHubTags and UntagHub all take HubNames — the plural list — which is how ELB Classic's AddTags, DescribeTags and RemoveTags take a load balancer. The read exports the singular name, and `binds` wraps that one export in a one-element list so rule 1 can supply the plural member; every emitter then has to spell a list holding a bound expression. The tag structure is the ordinary {Key, Value} and the untag member a plain string list, so the only axis this resource moves is the identifier's own shape — detectTagShape's two axes stay isolated on `gauge` and `valve`. The tag listing is read at $.TagDescriptions[0].Tags, which is where ELB's DescribeTags puts it.

Requires the pre-existing gauge, whose read runs in setup and whose ARN the sprocket records. The create is verified by an authored assertion instead of the derived read-back, and `async` wraps that authored clause — it calls the service again — while leaving the responseField clause beside it alone.
